thread.title: Should Stagnant iPhone Sales Worry Investors? - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)

author: Louis Stevens
title: Should Stagnant iPhone Sales Worry Investors? - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)
text:
What’s Weighing on the Stock Price? Apple’s ( AAPL ) stock has been rocked since reporting its fiscal year end numbers earlier this year. The numbers themselves were fantastic with revenue growth from iPhones hitting 29% year over year, total revenues growing 20%, and EPS growing 41% ; however, certain factors such as eliminating iPhone unit reporting has created uncertainty for investors.
The news that they will not be reporting unit sales has not been the only factor weighing on the share price, for as the saying goes, “When it rains it pours.” Numerous other factors have entered into the equation, not least of which is a slowing global economy and a fed that may create contagion through policy missteps.
So what do I see as the primary factors weighing on the share price? I see four primary factors, and they are below in order of what I perceive to be the least important to what I see to be the most important. I will address each before I get into why I’m now a buyer of the stock.
Qualcomm injunction U.S. - China Trade War Stagnant iPhone Sales and the new reporting method Policy missteps by the Fed and slowing global growth Qualcomm Injunction Qualcomm ( QCOM ) was recently granted preliminary injunctions against four Chinese subsidiaries of Apple, claiming that a series of iPhones sold in China infringed on two of Qualcomm’s patents. Despite China granting the injunctions, Apple iPhones have continued to be sold in China as usual. Apple claims that a simple software update will clear the air of any notion that they are selling phones afoul of patents held by Qualcomm. “Following China granting Qualcomm an import and sales ban on some iPhone models earlier this week, Apple announced this evening that it will release a software update to resolve any potential patent infringement.”
In my opinion, the case is rather cut and dry, and I suspect we won’t hear much about it in a few months or even less. Rumors and temporary setbacks for companies create investing opportunities all the time, although it’s incumbent on the individual investor to determine the truth behind the rumor and the degree to which the setback will impact the company. In the case of the Qualcomm Injunction, it seems highly apparent that investors, Apple, and Qualcomm will have forgotten it ever happened eventually.
U.S. – China Trade War The trade war has proven to have specific implications for each company; therefore, we must determine the unique set of circumstances each company faces in light of the ongoing trade war. For Apple, its set of circumstances is truly unique in that its footprint in China has become massive relatively speaking.
Apple has found itself caught in the crossfire of the trade war. In November, President Trump threatened to impose a 10% tariff on all Apple products imported from China. Such a move would likely cause a few different supply and demand dynamics to play out.
The cost of Apple products would likely rise as Apple would be forced to pass along the cost of importing products to the American consumer. As a result, the demand for Apple products would likely wane to some degree, the idea of which has caused downward pressure on the share price. "Bank of America Merrill Lynch said that a 25 percent tariff 'could be materially demand destructive' and estimates that about a third of the $26 billion it earns from those products comes from the United States."
With demand waning in America, Chinese manufactures could see their businesses hit and that could cause workers to be laid off as the result. As you can see, it’s a somewhat long and winding road before the Chinese are marginally impacted by the potential tariff on imported Apple products; meanwhile, the U.S. consumer would likely immediately bear the 10% tariff and resulting increase in product prices.
With the negatives to U.S. consumers in mind, it seems highly unlikely that President Trump will move forward with this tariff as it would hurt U.S. consumers to a greater degree than it would hurt Chinese manufacturers and workers. Apple reiterated by perspective by stating, "It is difficult to see how tariffs that hurt U.S. companies and U.S. consumers will advance the Government's objectives with respect to China's technology policies," Apple said. "We hope, instead, that you will reconsider these measures and work to find other, more effective solutions that leave the U.S. economy and U.S. consumer stronger and healthier than ever before."
Additionally, China shouldn’t be keen on damaging Apple as a means of retaliation, as Apple employs approximately 5 million Chinese workers and is a beloved product and status symbol in the nation of China.
Stagnant iPhone Sales And The New Reporting Method Next, we were recently confronted with the specter of less transparency in the way Apple reports its iPhone sales. Prior to the creation of the SEC in the 1930s, companies were extremely opaque and often did not report materially important data for investors to make informed decisions. Financial malfeasance was rampant, and investors were often misled.
After the great depression, the SEC was formed with the following mission: "The SEC requires public companies to disclose meaningful financial and other information to the public. This provides a common pool of knowledge for all investors to use to judge for themselves whether to buy, sell, or hold a particular security. Only through the steady flow of timely, comprehensive, and accurate information can people make sound investment decisions."
Evidently, Apple needs a history lesson to remind it as to why investors need vital data. Nevertheless, we believe a bull case can still be made, regardless of iPhone sales growth, or lack thereof.
Source: Statista.com
For the last several years, iPhone sales have found themselves pretty much stagnant, as the chart above illustrates. However, revenue from iPhone sales grew 29% in the last year alone , which means all present revenue growth from iPhones is the result of higher ASPs. There’s only so much ASPs can rise, though they’ve proven to be able to rise more than I would say many have speculated. Nobody can be certain as to the elasticity of the iPhone, and it is evident that Apple is trying to, with the release of its lower price XR, identify the exact points at which demand accelerates and decelerates.
From a positive perspective, the new reporting metric may be a way for Apple to begin to emphasize to its shareholding audience that they are diversifying away from being the one-trick, though highly lucrative, pony they’ve become through the iPhone. Although, I feel, in light of my discussion about the SEC's mandate, that such a sentiment is a bit of a stretch.
Source: Statista.com
Federal Reserve Policy Missteps "The job of the Federal Reserve,” William Martin famously said, is "to take away the punch bowl just as the party gets going.” If the Fed acts too aggressively in raising rates and transitioning from QE to QT, then the U.S. economy and certainly the economies abroad may grind into a slowdown. As debt becomes more expensive, servicing it and getting more becomes difficult and that could result in systematic risk for all participants in the economy, especially the consumer.
Additionally, a strengthening dollar, c reated by the Fed’s unwind of it balance sheet and rising fed funds rate, could cause contagion throughout the global economy . Such a dynamic has already reared its head in certain emerging market countries in which debt is denominated in U.S. dollars. Even without a global economic slowdown created by a strengthening dollar, international consumers will be less apt to buy an iPhone if its price increases for them as their currency weakens against the U.S. dollar.
Current Valuation At present, consensus estimates for Apple’s 2019 EPS hover at around $13.35, which implies a forward PE of about 12.3 with a share price of $165. If President Trump's tariffs were to be implemented, then forecasts might marginally decline as a result of the negative impacts the tariffs could cause . However, as I asserted earlier in the article, I see such a threat as cheap talk at best. It is most likely just ill-advised saber rattling in my opinion.
Source: Nasdaq.com
Additionally, analysts project Apple’s revenue to only grow at a rate around 5% in 2019. This is dramatically lower than the previous year, 2017-2018, during which Apple’s revenues grew approximately 20% and EPS grew 41% as a result of higher ASPs, growing services segment, and strong demand for the Apple Watch.
Source: Money.CNN.com
Apple’s projected level of top line growth of 5% merits a value PE multiple, and admittedly, Apple's present valuation seems warranted given the EPS and revenue data I just presented; however, I don’t believe the current valuation accounts for the potential for Apple to employ its many levers that will trigger share price appreciation.
As reference, I want to include a historic picture of how Apple has been valued.
As can be seen, Apple has hit significant rough patches in the past, especially around 2015, when revenues actually declined. This historic point of reference implies that there may be further room for the share price to fall; however, the following positives should create a floor, off which the share price will eventually rebound.
The Bull Case: Cash, Customers, Buybacks, Dividends and 5G Massive cash reserves Stable, growing free cash flow Share repurchase program Increasing Dividend Brand loyalty from customers The Advent of 5G In May, I began buying Apple hand over fist and set share to DRIP. Why? For several financial reasons outside of my belief that iPhone demand will persist, and Apple will lead in the next revolution of personal tech through wearables and AR.
Massive Cash Reserves Apple currently sits atop a cash stockpile of $237 billion. With this kind of capital, which will continue to grow in lockstep with Apple’s large margins and free cash flow, they could, to a limited extent, grow their share price without any organic growth at all. Though this may not be ideal, it provides justification for holding the stock while we await Apple's next innovative product or idea.
Source: Apple's 10-K
As the table above illustrates, Apple has a massive treasure chest, containing the aforementioned $237 billion. In conjunction with their, similarly, enormous free cash flow, management could take a number of routes in judiciously returning capital to shareholders.
Stable, Growing Free Cash Flow In the fiscal year ending September 30th, 2018, Apple generated approximately $77 billion in operating cash flow. The company’s capital expenditures were $16.7 billion during 2018; therefore, their free cash flow came in at about $60 billion for Apple's fiscal year 2018. Further, the company actually plans to reduce capex, thereby increasing free cash flow next year with revenues growing at around 5%.
"The Company anticipates utilizing approximately $14.0 billion for capital expenditures during 2019 , which includes product tooling and manufacturing process equipment; data centers; corporate facilities and infrastructure, including information systems hardware, software and enhancements; and retail store facilities." To put it concisely, the company generates unfathomable levels of cold hard cash, and as management has demonstrated, they plan to continue to return that money to their loyal shareholders.
Source: YCharts.com
Not only has the company demonstrated their commitment to returning capital to its shareholders, it's plainly stated it in its most recent 10-K. " The Company currently anticipates the cash used for future dividends, the share repurchase program and debt repayments will come from its current cash and cash generated from ongoing operating activities."
Share Repurchase Program In May of 2018, Apple announced a massive share buyback program to the tune of $100 billion. Apple has been executing on this program, and with lower share prices, the execution will likely prove to be valuable to its shareholders. According to their most recent 10-k, they're about 33% through the execution of the $100 billion buyback.
Source: Apple 10-K
There are a couple takeaways from the above snippet from Apple's most recent 10-K. 1) They still have $71 billion dollars worth of shares to repurchase. 2) They bought the first $29 billion much higher than where stock currently trades. And 2) market weakness will create fantastic opportunities to deploy cash at significantly lower share prices.
So what would $71 billion dollars worth of share repurchases look like, mathematically, for Apple's bottom line?
Apple currently has approximately 5 billion shares outstanding, with which they calculate their EPS as can be seen below. If Apple were to buy back their shares at an average of $165 with the remainder of their current repurchase program ($71B), then they would reduce their float by approximately 430,000,000 shares. According to my very basic calculations, such a repurchase alone would result in an increase in EPS of approximately 8.3%.
As Apple continues its committed track of repurchasing shares as a means of returning dollars to shareholders, EPS will continue to benefit, which will push the share price higher.
Increasing Dividend Management has made it expressly clear that they now intend to raise the dividend yearly. Currently, Apple pays a yearly dividend of $2.92, which represents a cash payout ratio (dividend/fcf) of 21.8%. "On May 1, 2018, the Company also announced the Board of Directors raised the Company’s quarterly cash dividend from $0.63 to $0.73 per share, beginning with the dividend paid during the third quarter of 2018. The Company intends to increase its dividend on an annual basis, subject to declaration by the Board of Directors."
Customer Brand Loyalty Ensuring Stable FCF So long as customers remain loyal to Apple, they will continue to generate massive free cash flow, much of which, as I've shared, they will return to their shareholders through buybacks and dividends. According to a recent survey conducted by Telsyte , “Apple [retains] very strong customer loyalty, with 90 per cent of iPhone owners saying they plan to buy another iPhone. But people who bought phones from Chinese manufacturers such as Oppo, ZTE and Huawei said they didn't plan to repeat the experience, with only 13 per cent saying they would buy another Chinese-made phone, down from 20 per cent the same time a year ago.”
Source: Businessinsider.com
Loyalty to the Apple brand is unparalleled, despite increases in the prices of their products. Brand loyalty is a central factor in my thesis in which management's commitment to judiciously returning money to shareholders will continue to drive price appreciation. Without such loyalty, Apple's enormous cash flows and cash reserves would come into question, but with it, the company represents a money printing machine for its shareholders.
The Advent of 5G I’d like to mention the advent of 5G as a component of my bullish thesis, which is expected to reach consumers in flagship smart phones in 2020. I see 5G as a potential catalyst for a revitalization of iPhone sales; in that, current smart phones are not compatible with 5G networks, and new phones must be purchased in order to enjoy the benefits of 5G.
"It is important to note that 5G is not an incremental or backward-compatible update to existing mobile communications standards. 5G is separate from 4G standards like LTE or WiMAX, and cannot be delivered to existing phones, tablets, or wireless modems by means of tower upgrades or software updates," reports James Sanders of TechRepublic.
In Australia, a study was conducted in which they found that there may be "Pent-Up Demand" for smartphones at the moment. “…one in every three Australians is planning to put off upgrading their smartphone until 5G is available, said Telsyte managing director Foad Fadaghi , the author of the report.” Consumers’ plans to delay purchasing an iPhone until some new revolutionary tech, namely 5G, reaches the market could create pent-up demand that would be a boon for smart phone makers by 2020.
I predict that Apple will capitalize on this new technology aggressively, and it seems likely to me that iPhone sales will benefit greatly as holdout owners of old phones transition to the new network. “That overall decline in sales could get worse once Australians decide to wait for 5G, 'but conversely we will likely see a strong pick-up once 5G networks and handsets come to market, meeting the pent-up demand,' Mr Fadaghi told The Australian Financial Review .” I believe we can expect the same to occur in the U.S.
Takeaway: Buy on Market Weakness and Set to DRIP Apple is presently facing headwinds in the form of fear and uncertainty. As the old adage goes, "Buy when there's blood in the streets." And as of December 2018, there is certainly blood in the streets.
Although Apple may not be in the hands of the great innovator that was Steve Jobs any longer, current management has declared their commitment to returning capital to investors. “We generated $19.5 billion in operating cash flow and returned over $23 billion to shareholders in dividends and share repurchases in the September quarter, bringing total capital returned in fiscal 2018 to almost $90 billion," said Luca Maestri, Apple’s CFO.
And with stable brand loyalty that exceeds any of its competitors by a wide margin, the enormous free cash flow and the resulting return of capital to shareholders will only persist.
Disclosure: I am/we are long AAPL. I wrote this article myself, and it expresses my own opinions. I am not receiving compensation for it (other than from Seeking Alpha). I have no business relationship with any company whose stock is mentioned in this article.
